questions.stem: The International Labour Organization, founded in 1919, is distinctive among UN agencies because its decisions involve which groups?
options: Governments only, voting by population size in an annual assembly
Trade unions only, who elect the members of its governing body
Employers only, through their national chambers of commerce
Governments, employers and workers, in a tripartite structure
questions.explanation: The ILO brings together representatives of governments, employers and workers, so labour standards are negotiated by all three. Its conventions, such as those on freedom of association and collective bargaining, recognise core workers' rights in international law.

questions.stem: The Harvester case (1907) is significant in Australian workplace law because Justice Higgins:
options: set a 'fair and reasonable' wage based on the needs of an unskilled worker supporting a family
ruled that employers could pay any wage the market allowed, without any statutory minimum
abolished conciliation and arbitration and replaced it with individual workplace contracts
held that women must be paid the same wage as men for work of equal value in all Australian industries
questions.explanation: In Ex parte H V McKay, Justice Higgins based a fair and reasonable wage on what an unskilled labourer needed to support a family, which became the basis of the basic wage. Equal pay for work of equal value came decades later, and the case strengthened rather than abolished arbitration.

questions.stem: Mia's employer has underpaid her for months. Which body's main role is to investigate this, help her recover the money and take the employer to court if needed?
options: The Australian Human Rights Commission
The Fair Work Ombudsman
The Fair Work Commission
SafeWork NSW
questions.explanation: The Fair Work Ombudsman educates, investigates breaches of workplace laws and can litigate in the courts to recover underpayments and seek penalties. The Fair Work Commission is the national workplace relations tribunal: it sets minimum wages and awards, approves agreements and hears unfair dismissal claims.

questions.stem: Why is a nurse employed by a NSW public hospital generally covered by the NSW Industrial Relations Commission rather than the Fair Work Commission?
options: The Fair Work Act applies only to employees in the mining and manufacturing industries
Health workers are excluded from all Australian workplace laws by the Constitution
The NSW Industrial Relations Commission hears all employment disputes in New South Wales
NSW did not refer its industrial powers over its own public sector to the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: NSW referred most of its industrial relations powers to the Commonwealth in 2009, but kept the state public sector and local government in the state system under the NSW Industrial Relations Commission. Most private sector employees in NSW are covered by the Fair Work Act.

questions.stem: Jake is told he is an 'independent contractor', but he works set shifts, wears the company uniform, uses its tools and cannot send anyone else to do his work. Since 2024, how is his status decided under the Fair Work Act?
options: By the label in his written contract, which settles the question if both parties signed it
By whether he holds an ABN, because anyone with an ABN is legally a contractor
By whether he is paid weekly, because weekly pay always indicates employment
By the real substance, practical reality and true nature of the relationship as a whole
questions.explanation: Section 15AA of the Fair Work Act, in force from 26 August 2024, requires courts to look at the real substance, practical reality and true nature of the relationship, including how it works in practice. This reversed the focus on the written contract that followed two 2022 High Court decisions, so a label or an ABN does not decide the question.

questions.stem: A cleaning company dismisses its employees and immediately re-engages them as 'contractors' doing the same work. What is this conduct called under the Fair Work Act?
options: Sham contracting
Labour hire work
Outworking
Redeployment
questions.explanation: Sham contracting is misrepresenting an employment relationship as independent contracting, or dismissing an employee to re-engage them as a contractor for the same work, and it is prohibited. Employers do it to avoid paying minimum wages, leave and superannuation.

questions.stem: A food delivery rider works through an app and is not an employee. What protection has the Fair Work Act offered such workers since 2024?
options: The Fair Work Commission can make minimum standards orders for employee-like workers on digital platforms
Every gig worker is now automatically treated as a permanent full-time employee of the platform company they use
Gig workers must be paid the same hourly rate as the platform's executives under equal pay laws
The rider can claim all NES leave entitlements, including annual leave and long service leave
questions.explanation: Reforms in 2024 created the category of 'employee-like' workers performing digital platform work, and the Fair Work Commission can set minimum standards for them, such as pay and insurance. They remain independent contractors, so they do not become employees with NES leave.

questions.stem: Lucy's written employment contract gives her fewer days of annual leave than the National Employment Standards. What is the legal effect?
options: The NES still applies, because a contract cannot provide less than the minimum standards
The contract applies, because Lucy agreed to its terms when she signed it voluntarily
The contract applies unless Lucy can show she was pressured into signing it by her employer
The NES applies only if Lucy is a member of a trade union covered by an agreement
questions.explanation: The NES, modern awards and enterprise agreements set minimums that a contract cannot undercut, so Lucy keeps her NES entitlements whatever she signed. A contract can provide better conditions than the safety net, but not worse.

questions.stem: Before the Fair Work Commission approves an enterprise agreement, it must be satisfied that the agreement passes the better off overall test. What does this test require?
options: The employer would be better off financially under the agreement than under the relevant modern award, overall
Every single term of the agreement must be more generous than the matching term of the award
Most employees would be better off, even if some would be worse off than under the award
Each employee would be better off overall under the agreement than under the relevant modern award
questions.explanation: The better off overall test (BOOT) compares the agreement with the relevant modern award and requires each award-covered employee, and prospective employee, to be better off overall. Some terms can be less generous if others make up for them, so a line-by-line comparison is not required.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of trade unions in advocating for workers' rights?
options: They bargain collectively for agreements, represent members in disputes and campaign for reform
They enforce the Fair Work Act and can fine employers that underpay their union members
They approve enterprise agreements and decide unfair dismissal claims for their members
They set the national minimum wage each year after consulting employers and governments
questions.explanation: Unions bargain for enterprise agreements, represent members in disputes and before the Fair Work Commission, and campaign for law reform. Enforcement and fines belong to the Fair Work Ombudsman and the courts, and approving agreements and setting the minimum wage are Fair Work Commission functions.

questions.stem: In 2015 a joint Four Corners and Fairfax investigation revealed widespread underpayment of workers, many of them international students, at 7-Eleven stores. What does this show about the role of the media?
options: It has the legal power to order franchisors to repay their franchisees' workers
It mainly reports on workplace issues only after courts have already decided them
It can expose hidden exploitation and prompt regulatory and legislative responses
It is the main way underpaid workers recover their wages through the legal system
questions.explanation: The investigation brought hidden wage exploitation to public attention and was followed by a Fair Work Ombudsman inquiry and new laws making some franchisors responsible for underpayments in their networks. The media cannot order repayment; workers still rely on the Ombudsman, the courts and the business.

questions.stem: Under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW), what is the primary duty of a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU)?
options: To ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and others
To guarantee that no worker will ever suffer any injury or illness at the workplace
To ensure the health and safety of workers only while they are physically on the employer's premises
To pay compensation to injured workers, but not to take steps to prevent injuries
questions.explanation: The primary duty of care requires a PCBU to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and others affected by the work, including psychological health. It is not an absolute guarantee, and it extends beyond the employer's premises to wherever the work is done.

questions.stem: A company director never asks about safety, does not know the hazards of the business and provides no resources for safety. Which duty under the WHS Act is the director most likely breaching?
options: The officer's duty to exercise due diligence
The worker's duty to take reasonable care
The duty of other persons at the workplace
The duty of a health and safety representative
questions.explanation: Officers, such as directors, must exercise due diligence to ensure the PCBU complies with its duties, which includes keeping up to date with safety matters, understanding the operations and hazards, and ensuring resources are provided. A worker's duty is to take reasonable care for their own and others' safety and to follow reasonable safety instructions.

questions.stem: A trained health and safety representative sees workers using a scaffold that she believes is about to collapse. What power does she have under the WHS Act?
options: She can fine the business on the spot and order the arrest of the responsible manager
She can close the whole business permanently without any further review by the regulator
She has no powers and can only report her concerns to the business at the next meeting
She can direct that the unsafe work cease and can issue a provisional improvement notice
questions.explanation: An elected health and safety representative who has completed approved training can direct that unsafe work cease where there is a serious risk, and can issue a provisional improvement notice requiring a contravention to be fixed. Fines and prosecutions are matters for the regulator and the courts.

questions.stem: A SafeWork NSW inspector finds an unguarded machine that poses a serious and immediate risk of injury. Which notice is most appropriate?
options: A compliance notice requiring the business to pay back its workers
A penalty notice for parking in a restricted area at the workplace
A prohibition notice stopping the activity until the risk is fixed
An improvement notice giving the business a year to fix the risk
questions.explanation: A prohibition notice stops an activity that involves a serious risk to health or safety until the risk is remedied. An improvement notice requires a contravention to be fixed within a set time, and a compliance notice is a Fair Work Ombudsman tool for unpaid wages.

questions.stem: A worker dies after a business owner knowingly ignores repeated warnings about a deadly hazard. What can the NSW WHS Act now provide in a case like this?
options: A warning letter only, because SafeWork NSW cannot take matters involving a death to court
A fine only, because imprisonment is not available for any offence in the WHS legislation
A prosecution for industrial manslaughter, with imprisonment of up to 25 years for an individual
A civil claim only, because deaths at work cannot lead to any criminal charges under the WHS Act
questions.explanation: NSW added an industrial manslaughter offence to the WHS Act in 2024, with a maximum of 25 years' imprisonment for an individual and a very large fine for a body corporate. It responds to criticism that penalties were too weak to deter conduct causing workplace deaths.

questions.stem: Why did all Australian jurisdictions, including NSW, prohibit the use of engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs from 1 July 2024?
options: Its manufacture breached competition laws because a single company made it
Cutting it releases silica dust that causes silicosis, an incurable lung disease
It was found to be flammable and had caused several large building fires
It was too expensive for most consumers, so builders refused to install it
questions.explanation: Workers cutting and polishing engineered stone breathe in respirable crystalline silica, which causes silicosis, and cases rose sharply among young stonemasons. The ban shows how regulation can lag behind new products and how WHS laws respond when other controls prove inadequate.

questions.stem: A business makes changes that greatly increase workloads and leaves bullying complaints unanswered. Why can this breach the WHS Act even though no-one is physically injured?
options: The WHS Act covers physical injuries only, but workers can claim under contract law
Workload is always a matter for the employee, so only the bullying can be relevant
Bullying complaints must be made to the police, so the business has no duty to act
The duty covers psychological health, and these are psychosocial hazards the business must manage
questions.explanation: Health under the WHS Act includes psychological health, and PCBUs must identify and control psychosocial hazards such as excessive workloads, bullying and harassment. Consulting workers, including in a culturally responsive way, is part of managing these risks.

questions.stem: From 1 January 2025, when can an employer commit a criminal offence under the Fair Work Act for underpaying an employee?
options: When it intentionally engages in conduct that results in a failure to pay the amount owed
Whenever it makes any underpayment, including a genuine mistake in a payroll system
Only when the underpayment exceeds the employee's total annual salary by a set amount
Only if the employee is a casual worker who is aged under 21 at the time of the underpayment
questions.explanation: The wage theft offence in section 327A applies where an employer intentionally engages in conduct resulting in a failure to pay amounts owed, and individuals can face up to 10 years' imprisonment. Honest mistakes are dealt with through civil remedies, such as back-payment and civil penalties, rather than the criminal law.

questions.stem: A Fair Work Inspector believes a restaurant has underpaid its staff. What can the inspector issue that requires the employer to calculate and pay the amounts owed?
options: A compliance notice
A prohibition notice
A provisional improvement notice
A certificate of conciliation
questions.explanation: A compliance notice requires the employer to fix a contravention, for example by back-paying wages, and failing to comply can lead to court action. Prohibition notices and provisional improvement notices are WHS tools for safety risks.

questions.stem: A cafe asks Ella to work a 'trial' of three full unpaid shifts serving customers before it decides whether to hire her. Which is correct?
options: This is lawful, as long as the cafe gives her free meals during each of the three trial shifts
This is unlawful only if the cafe is a large business with more than 100 employees on staff
This is unlawful, because an unpaid trial must be no longer than needed to show her skills and be supervised
This is lawful, because an employer can require any number of unpaid trial shifts before hiring
questions.explanation: According to the Fair Work Ombudsman, an unpaid trial is lawful only if it is necessary to demonstrate the person's skills, lasts only as long as needed for that, and is under direct supervision. Three full shifts of serving customers is productive work, so Ella must be paid.

questions.stem: Why can a university student complete an unpaid placement at a law firm without breaching the Fair Work Act?
options: All work done by students under 25 is exempt from the minimum wage provisions
Law firms are excluded from the Fair Work Act because they are professional bodies
The student has agreed in writing to work for no pay, which always makes it lawful
It is a vocational placement required as part of an authorised education course
questions.explanation: A vocational placement that is a requirement of an authorised education or training course, and for which the person is not entitled to pay, is not employment under the Fair Work Act. A written agreement to work for nothing does not override minimum wage obligations in a genuine employment relationship.

questions.stem: Without asking her, a shop deducts money from Zara's wages to cover a shortfall in the cash register at the end of her shift. Is this deduction lawful?
options: Yes, because employees are always responsible for cash shortfalls that occur while they are on shift
Yes, as long as the amount deducted is less than the employee's casual loading for that week
No, but only because the shop failed to report the shortfall to the police before deducting it
No, because deductions generally need written authorisation and must be principally for the employee's benefit
questions.explanation: Under the Fair Work Act, an employer can generally deduct money only if the employee authorises it in writing and it is principally for the employee's benefit, or if an award, agreement, law or court order allows it. Recovering a till shortfall benefits the employer, so this is an unlawful deduction.

questions.stem: Kai discovers his co-worker is paid more for the same job and tells her what he earns. His contract has a clause forbidding him to disclose his pay. What is the legal position?
options: Kai can be dismissed for serious misconduct because he breached his employment contract
The secrecy clause is valid, but only for employees who earn more than the minimum wage
Kai may disclose his pay only to a union official and not to any of his co-workers
Kai has a protected right to disclose his pay, and the secrecy clause has no effect
questions.explanation: Since December 2022, the Fair Work Act gives employees a workplace right to disclose, or not disclose, their pay and conditions, and pay secrecy terms have no effect. The change aims to help workers identify gender pay gaps and underpayment.

questions.stem: Under the NES, how much paid annual leave does a full-time employee accrue each year?
options: 10 days, the same as for personal leave
4 weeks, or 5 weeks for certain shiftworkers
2 weeks, or 3 weeks for certain shiftworkers
6 weeks, or 8 weeks for certain shiftworkers
questions.explanation: The NES provides 4 weeks of paid annual leave per year of service for full-time employees, pro rata for part-time employees, and 5 weeks for certain shiftworkers. Casual employees do not receive paid annual leave and are paid a casual loading instead.

questions.stem: How much paid personal/carer's leave does a full-time employee receive each year under the NES?
options: 20 days
10 days
5 days
15 days
questions.explanation: Full-time employees accrue 10 days of paid personal/carer's leave each year, and part-time employees accrue it pro rata. It covers personal illness or injury and caring for an immediate family or household member.

questions.stem: Sophie, a casual employee, needs time off after her grandmother dies. What is she entitled to under the NES?
options: 10 days of unpaid leave, the same as family violence leave
2 days of unpaid compassionate leave for the occasion
2 days of paid compassionate leave for the occasion
No leave, because casual employees have no NES leave rights
questions.explanation: Compassionate leave is 2 days per permissible occasion, such as the death of an immediate family or household member, and grandparents are immediate family. It is paid for full-time and part-time employees but unpaid for casuals.

questions.stem: Which statement about family and domestic violence leave under the NES is correct?
options: It is available only to employees who have worked for 12 months or more
Employees, including casuals, can take 10 days of paid leave in a 12-month period
Only full-time employees can take 5 days of unpaid leave in any 12-month period at work
Employees can take unlimited unpaid leave, but only with a court order
questions.explanation: Since 2023, all employees, including part-time and casual employees, can access 10 days of paid family and domestic violence leave in a 12-month period, replacing the earlier entitlement of 5 days of unpaid leave. It is available in full from the start of employment rather than accruing.

questions.stem: Dan has worked full-time for his employer for three years and is about to become a parent. How do the NES and the government's Paid Parental Leave scheme work together?
options: He is not eligible for any parental leave because only birth mothers can take leave under the NES
He can take up to 12 months of unpaid leave under the NES and may separately receive government-funded parental leave pay
The NES requires his employer to pay him his full salary for 12 months while he cares for the new child
He must choose between NES parental leave and government pay, because the two cannot be combined
questions.explanation: Eligible employees, including fathers and partners, can take up to 12 months of unpaid parental leave under the NES and request up to 12 more months, which the employer can refuse only on reasonable business grounds. Paid Parental Leave is a separate government-funded payment that can be received during that unpaid leave.

questions.stem: Rosa has worked for the same NSW employer for 10 years. Which law gives her an entitlement to long service leave?
options: The Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), which gives 4 weeks of leave after 10 years of service
The Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW), which gives 6 months of paid leave after 10 years
No law, because long service leave depends entirely on her employer's personal policy
The Long Service Leave Act 1955 (NSW), which gives 2 months of paid leave after 10 years
questions.explanation: The NES lists long service leave, but for most NSW workers the entitlement comes from the Long Service Leave Act 1955 (NSW): 2 months of paid leave after 10 years of continuous service, with further leave for each additional 5 years. Some awards and agreements provide their own long service leave terms.

questions.stem: Why is the growth of casual work a challenge for the regulation of leave, and what measure addresses it?
options: Casuals receive more paid leave than permanent staff, so their hours have been capped by law
Casuals cannot take any leave at all, so all casual employment has been prohibited since 2024
Casuals must be given permanent jobs after one week, so they lose their right to choose shifts
Casuals miss out on paid annual and personal leave, so they get a loading and a pathway to permanent work
questions.explanation: Casual employees receive a casual loading, usually 25 per cent under awards, instead of paid annual and personal leave, which leaves many without paid time off. Under the employee choice pathway, an eligible casual can notify their employer that they want to convert to permanent employment after 6 months, or 12 months with a small business.

questions.stem: An employer refuses to promote Anika because she is pregnant. Under the Fair Work Act's general protections, what is this?
options: Adverse action taken because of a protected attribute
A genuine redundancy based on operational needs
A lawful exercise of the employer's management rights
An unfair dismissal that must go to the Local Court
questions.explanation: The general protections prohibit adverse action, such as refusing a promotion or dismissing someone, because of attributes including pregnancy, sex, race, age and disability. She could also complain under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) or the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW).

questions.stem: A worker in NSW wants to make a complaint of age discrimination under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW). What is the usual pathway?
options: A complaint directly to the High Court of Australia, which hears all discrimination cases
A complaint to SafeWork NSW, which can order the employer to pay compensation on the spot
A complaint to the police, because all age discrimination is a criminal offence in NSW
A complaint to Anti-Discrimination NSW for conciliation, then NCAT if it is not resolved
questions.explanation: Complaints under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) go first to Anti-Discrimination NSW, which investigates and tries to resolve them by conciliation; unresolved complaints can be referred to NCAT. Discrimination complaints are civil matters, not criminal ones.

questions.stem: How did the positive duty inserted into the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) in 2022 change employers' obligations?
options: Employers must now pay a fixed fine to every employee who makes a complaint of sexual harassment
Employers are no longer liable for harassment, because the duty has been transferred to the police
Employers must dismiss any employee accused of sexual harassment, without an investigation
Employers must take reasonable and proportionate measures to prevent sexual harassment, not just respond to complaints
questions.explanation: Following the Respect@Work report, the positive duty requires employers to take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate sex discrimination and sexual harassment as far as possible, and the Australian Human Rights Commission can enforce it. Previously the law relied mainly on individuals making complaints after harm had occurred.

questions.stem: Omar has worked for a large company for two years and is dismissed without warning over a minor mistake. What must he show in an unfair dismissal claim?
options: The employer intended to discriminate against him because of a protected attribute he has
The employer committed a criminal offence when it decided to end his employment
He was dismissed in breach of the minimum wage, so he is owed back pay
The dismissal was harsh, unjust or unreasonable and was not a case of genuine redundancy
questions.explanation: An unfair dismissal is a dismissal that is harsh, unjust or unreasonable and is not a genuine redundancy (and, for a small business, not consistent with the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code). He has served more than the minimum employment period of 6 months for a large business, or 12 months for a small one.

questions.stem: Within what time must an employee usually lodge an unfair dismissal application with the Fair Work Commission?
options: 21 days after the dismissal takes effect
6 months after the dismissal takes effect
12 months after the dismissal takes effect
7 days after the dismissal takes effect
questions.explanation: Unfair dismissal applications, and general protections claims involving dismissal, must be lodged within 21 days, and the Commission extends this only in exceptional circumstances. The short time limit is itself a barrier for workers who do not know their rights.

questions.stem: A company says Ben's job is redundant, but it hires someone else to do the same role a week later, and it had a vacant position he could have filled. Why is this unlikely to be a genuine redundancy?
options: The job was still needed and redeployment would have been reasonable, so the redundancy is not genuine
A redundancy is genuine only if the employer has first obtained approval from Ben's union
A redundancy is genuine only if the business is about to close down within twelve months
A redundancy is genuine only if Ben agreed in writing that his job was no longer needed
questions.explanation: A redundancy is genuine only if the employer no longer requires the job to be done by anyone because of changes in operational requirements, it complied with any consultation obligations, and redeployment was not reasonable. Hiring a replacement shows the job still existed, so Ben may bring an unfair dismissal claim.

questions.stem: In most unfair dismissal claims, what is the first step in resolving the dispute at the Fair Work Commission?
options: A conciliation conference, where a conciliator helps the parties reach an agreement
A jury trial in the Federal Court to decide whether the employer has acted unfairly
An automatic order for reinstatement, without hearing from the employer
A criminal investigation of the employer by the Australian Federal Police
questions.explanation: Most claims go first to a conciliation conference, a form of alternative dispute resolution that is quick, cheap and confidential, and most settle there. If not, a Commission member can decide the matter; reinstatement is the primary remedy, with compensation where reinstatement is inappropriate.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest example of a barrier that stops vulnerable workers from using employment dispute resolution?
options: A temporary visa holder fears that complaining will cost her job and her right to stay
A permanent employee lodges a claim and attends a free conciliation conference
A union member asks the union to represent him at the Fair Work Commission
An employee uses the Fair Work Ombudsman's free online tools to check her pay
questions.explanation: Fear of victimisation, insecure visa status, limited English, cost and short time limits all discourage vulnerable workers from enforcing their rights. Free conciliation, union representation and the Ombudsman's tools are ways of reducing these barriers rather than barriers themselves.
